text: The enemy in this war film is frequently standing on the same side of the line. David Carr leaves unemployment in Britain for Spain in 1936 and signs on with the POUM militia, one faction in a coalition of liberals, communists and anarchists who have agreed to hold a front and agreed on very little else. Loach spends the film on what a militia actually does with its days: the shortage of rifles, the long meetings, the question of who owns a field now that the landlord has gone, argued at length by people who may be dead by Thursday. Then the orders begin arriving from Moscow. The European Film Award for Best Film went to it, which did nothing to soften the anger in the writing. 109 minutes, and none of it treats 1936 as a matter already settled.

Penang to Kuala Lumpur is a bus ride, and it is also the distance at which a family can no longer see what a daughter is doing. Ping comes south to work for an aunt, which means hours behind a counter and a room that belongs to somebody else. Then a young man called John starts turning up, and keeps turning up. Tan Chui Mui gives his approaches exactly the attention she gives the working day — the waiting, the small talk, the boyfriend still up north who is technically still hers — so that the shift from one life into another arrives without any announcement. Ninety minutes, in Chinese. The film's case is that a person can be walked into a whole future in steps so small that not one of them looks like a decision.

A hunter who can take an animal without spoiling the hide is useful to everyone, and that is where his difficulties start. Tizoc has the skill, along with the patience and the mildness that neighbours find harder to forgive than any of it, and the film watches envy gather around him. Mexican cinema in 1956 worked in a register where feeling is declared rather than implied, and Ismael Rodríguez stays inside it while making his subject a man whom other people are forever explaining to one another: what he knows, what he is owed, whom he may love. The Silver Bear went to the leading performance, and the picture is built so that a face has to carry the argument — 109 minutes of people deciding what to do about someone they cannot place.

Two hours and twenty-one minutes, most of it spent in the company of two people who love each other and are very hard to be near. A brother and sister, worn down in ways the film never pauses to diagnose, come back into each other's lives after years apart; that is the whole plot, and Cassavetes measures time in the length of a conversation rather than in incidents. Scenes carry on past the point where a script would cut. Somebody keeps talking after the point has been made, and the surplus is the information. It won the Golden Bear, which for a film with no event to sell is a strange and exactly right outcome. Nobody inside it is looking for a resolution; they are looking for company.

The arrangement takes one sentence to explain, which is why the film can spend an hour and three quarters not arriving at it: a yellow handkerchief in the window means come home. The man travelling towards that window has just come out of prison for murder, and he is not travelling alone — two strangers with a car take him along, and Hokkaido is wide enough to hold the three of them for days. Yamada plays most of it as comedy. The talk in the car stays light, the roads run on, the ex-wife is four years away and getting closer at driving speed, and nobody proposes discussing what may be waiting there. It took the Japan Academy Film Prize for Picture of the Year, and its method is a road courtesy: strangers agreeing not to ask the obvious question.

Blackmail is a strange way to recruit an athlete, and a professor is a strange person to be doing it. Shuhei is a college senior with something to lose, the school's sumo club is close to disbandment, and the two facts are introduced to each other. What keeps the comedy honest is that sumo lets nobody hide. The ring is small, a bout is over in seconds, and there is nowhere in it to be anyone other than oneself. Suō keeps the tone light without pretending the work is easy. The misfits around Shuhei stay bad at this for a long time. The Blue Ribbon Award for Best Picture came to it, and 105 minutes is about as long as the joke can bear weight.

A business in trouble does not announce itself; it arrives as a run of conversations a man cannot afford to end badly. Save the Tiger gives itself two days and a hundred minutes, and it uses that compression the way a stage play would: what has been deferred for years all falls due inside the same forty-eight hours. Nothing in it is spectacular. The Academy gave the film Best Actor, and on the evidence of the screenplay that is where the weight sits — long stretches in which one man talks himself into something out loud while another works out what is actually being proposed. The private life is not a subplot here. It is the thing the working day keeps putting off, until the two days run out of room.

A man who has spent his working life knowing exactly how paper is made discovers that this is not a transferable skill. The layoff comes early; what follows is the interviewing, and the particular humiliation of pricing himself for people with less experience than his last promotion. Park Chan-wook shoots it as comedy first, which is the least merciful option available, then lets the crime in slowly, through a side entrance. 139 minutes gives him room to count out the small refusals one by one, so that when the manager begins doing something unforgivable the arithmetic is already on the table. The Blue Dragon named it Best Film. Its subject is not the violence; its subject is the interview.

Two embassies in one city, sent by two states that do not recognise each other, and one road out. Somalia's civil war closes over Mogadishu while the North and South Korean missions are still busy competing; then the phones stop, the airport shuts, and the only workable plan requires each delegation to put itself in the other's hands. Ryoo Seung-wan keeps the diplomacy as concrete as the driving: who has fuel, whose signature still means anything, who rides with whom. The film went forward as Korea's submission to the Academy Awards. 121 minutes, and long before anyone is shot at, the emergency has already arrived as a question of protocol — which rules apply when the governments issuing them are unreachable and the staff on the ground have to agree on one way out.

Cecilia goes back to the same picture again and again because a ticket costs less than anything else that helps. New Jersey in the Depression, a waitress who is not much good at waitressing and who has just lost the job anyway, and up on the screen an adventure called The Purple Rose of Cairo in which nobody has money trouble and everyone speaks in finished sentences. Then the film she is watching begins to notice her. Allen runs the two worlds against each other for 82 minutes without letting either win the argument, and the screenplay, which took the Academy Award, is the reason the conceit never softens into whimsy: every consequence is worked through, the awkward ones included.

Two sisters, two men, and a set of theories about love that everyone involved intends to test in person. The setting is an English coalfield in the 1920s, used less as scenery than as the thing Gudrun and Ursula have decided will not govern them; the men are a rich one with nothing to do and one who theorises. Russell takes the talk seriously and then interrupts it with bodies. The pattern recurs: an idea about how people ought to belong to each other, then an afternoon that tests whether the idea survives contact. 131 minutes, and the Academy Award for cinematography is a fair signal of where part of the thinking happens — much of the arguing is done with light and place rather than with dialogue.

Kata is in her forties, works, keeps her own house, and has decided she wants a child; the man she has been seeing for years has a wife and no intention of helping. Mészáros films this without heat. The house, the workplace, the institution that has charge of the teenager Anna — each is laid out as a set of rules, and the two women meet across them almost by accident, the older one asked for a small favour and giving more than was asked for. What grows between them is not mothering, and nobody calls it friendship either. 88 minutes, in which the largest events are conversations, permissions and arrangements. It took the Golden Bear, which for a film this quiet about the paperwork of wanting somebody is worth saying out loud.
